Abstract:
<jats:p>Metals with a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure such as magnesium, titanium and zirconium constitute key structural materials in the aerospace, automotive, biomedical and nuclear energy industries. Their welding and regeneration by conventional methods is hindered due to the limited number of slip systems, high reactivity and susceptibility to the formation of defects. Laser technologies offer precise energy control, minimization of the heat-affected zone and the possibility of producing joints and coatings of high quality. This article constitutes a comprehensive review of the state of knowledge concerning laser welding, cladding and regeneration of HCP metals. The physical mechanisms of laser beam interactions are discussed including the dynamics of the keyhole channel, Marangoni flows and the formation of gas defects. The characteristics of the microstructure of joints are presented including the formation of α′ martensite in titanium, phase segregation in magnesium and hydride formation in zirconium. Particular attention is devoted to residual stresses, techniques of cladding protective coatings for nuclear energy with Accident Tolerant Fuel (ATF) and advanced numerical modeling using artificial intelligence. The perspectives for the development of technology are indicated including the concept of the digital twin and intelligent real-time process control systems.</jats:p>

The excerpt identifies powder particles, spatter, and residue accumulating on the LPBF optical window as contamination risks. Because the window separates the optical train from the chamber, contamination can compromise consistent laser delivery and therefore build quality; the text specifically emphasizes keeping the window dust-free and cooling it together with the optical system to maintain consistent output. The recommended protection is an airflow arrangement, such as a gas knife or down draft, to prevent powder and spatter from settling on the window. The window is also generally cleaned after every build to remove residue. The passage discusses filtration of inert gas carrying spatter, including optional cyclone separation and filters for particles larger than approximately 5–10 µm, but this relates to gas recirculation rather than a quantified optical-window contamination effect. It does not provide numerical values for focal shift or laser power loss caused by window contamination. It also does not specify a recommended cover-glass or cover-slide thickness. ## pqac-00000017

From text 'bonhoff2017experimentalandtheoretical pages 6-10'.

T Bonhoff, M Schniedenharn, and J Stollenwerk. Experimental and theoretical analysis of thermo-optical effects in protective window for selective laser melting. Unknown journal, 2017.

The excerpt evaluates contamination of an LPBF laser protective window by metal plume, which includes deposited spatter/condensate. Contamination increases the window’s absorptivity and produces thermally induced optical effects: a negative focal shift, increased beam waist, reduced beam quality, and stronger ring structures around the central Gaussian distribution, likely from thermal aberrations. In fused silica experiments at 400 W, progressively contaminated windows exhibited focal shifts of approximately −22 to −30 mm, while the waist radius increased from 35 µm to 53 µm. Simulations showed that an additional absorptivity of 0.5% produced comparable focal-shift and beam-waist changes. Cleaning the window nearly restored the original focus, confirming that contamination was responsible. The transmitted-power measurements suggest contamination absorptivity remained below an estimated 1% upper threshold; although contamination causes laser-power loss, the authors describe that loss as less important for component quality than the focal shift and beam-quality degradation. The excerpt does not provide recommendations concerning a gas knife, cover glass/cover slide thickness, or a quantitative comparison of spatter versus condensate effects. It therefore supports the need to limit contamination but cannot establish a specific protection configuration or thickness.

The excerpt indicates that recoater speed strongly affects powder-spreading quality. At low speeds, gravity and friction-driven rearrangement allow particles more time to reorganize, generally improving packing density and deposition uniformity. Increasing speed makes inertial effects more important, causing greater variability in layer density and thickness. High speeds are associated with reduced packing density, lower surface coverage, increased roughness, stronger segregation, local powder accumulation, and uncovered substrate regions. The problem is especially pronounced for fine, cohesive powders, where rapid motion can prevent complete rearrangement and create clusters and heterogeneous deposits. The excerpt does not provide a specific recommended recoater speed; it only states that industrial systems balance deposition quality against throughput. Regarding collisions, rigid metallic blades can mechanically interact with protruding particles or previously consolidated features, disturbing the layer and potentially interrupting the process. Flexible polymer blades accommodate minor geometric irregularities and reduce collision risk, while rollers compact powder and may produce denser beds but can increase segregation. The excerpt does not discuss blade wear or streaking specifically, nor does it identify spatter or curled parts as distinct collision causes. Therefore, no direct conclusion about wear, streaking, or an optimal numerical speed can be drawn from this passage.

The excerpt reports that recoater speed has no universally positive effect on powder-spreading quality. Most cited studies find that increasing recoating velocity reduces spreadability, although one contrasting study observed higher deposition rate and spreadability at higher velocity; this difference may be associated with powder cohesivity. For extremely cohesive powders, higher recoater velocity can generate shearing forces that break powder interlocking and improve deposition. Roller rotational speed should therefore be selected together with recoating velocity and powder flowability. In particular, a higher roller speed is recommended for overcoming poor powder flowability. Process maps can be used to balance layer roughness, porosity, throughput, recoating velocity, and roller speed. Regarding recoater material, the excerpt states that a high friction coefficient can cause powder particles to adhere to the recoater instead of being deposited, which can degrade spreading. The provided passage does not explain what causes recoater collisions with spatter or curled parts, does not discuss blade-material wear mechanisms, and does not specifically describe streaking. It also does not provide one universal recommended recoater speed for LPBF; the recommendation is condition-dependent, especially on powder flowability and cohesivity.

Triboelectric charging occurs during particle–particle collisions, segregation, and contact with spreading or container materials. It can make fine powder flow difficult and can produce nonuniform powder layers. For same-material powders with different size fractions, smaller particles tend to gain electrons and become negatively charged, while larger particles become positively charged. Charge-driven segregation can therefore alter local particle-size distributions and packing factors between layers, reducing powder-bed homogeneity and potentially causing inconsistent part quality. Charging increases with surface contact area and is influenced by particle shape, roughness, material type, contact force, velocity, pressure, temperature, humidity, and moisture. Lower relative humidity generally increases charge, whereas wet powder has lower charge than dry powder. The cited triboelectric series places aluminium toward the positive side relative to Teflon, gold, nickel, and steel, and toward the negative side relative to borosilicate glass. For metallic powders, the reported series orders Inconel 718, stainless-steel 316L, titanium, Ti-6Al-4V, aluminium alloy A357, and borosilicate glass from electro-negative to electro-positive. Thus, material selection, conductive/compatible spreading surfaces, and humidity or moisture control may reduce charging; the excerpt specifically indicates that minimizing or eliminating electrostatic charge improves mixture homogeneity.

Fine powders are expected to be difficult to handle because decreasing particle size increases specific surface area and strengthens van der Waals, electrostatic, surface-tension, and other interparticle forces; powders below approximately 10 μm may be dominated by van der Waals forces. These effects reduce flowability and can promote bridging, blockage, and inconsistent discharge through narrow slots. For hopper operation, the text recommends preventing stagnant zones and ratholes, potentially by reducing material level, using internal mechanical agitators or external vibrators, or enlarging the outlet. The excerpt compares thermally induced focus shifts for fused silica, N-BK7, and N-FK51A under contamination and 400 W laser power, but it does not provide data for sapphire or a 500 W operating condition. 2.1  Chamber and build platform


The high-pressure laser melting (HPLM) system was constructed upon a custom chamber (Parr
Instrument Company) with a maximum operating pressure of 1900 psig, and a cylindrical 2.5 inch
(diameter) by 6.5 inch (length) bore. The chamber features an oblong window ﬂange, a removable

Alignment between the laser’s focal plane and the powder bed is crucial for achieving uniform
quality across the entire build area; misalignment will cause a change in eﬀective laser spot size.
To this end, a kinematic positioning system, displayed in Figure 2, was devised to exactly
constrain the build platform while giving precise control of alignment with the focal plane. Two
spheres contact the cylindrical bore of the chamber. One adjustable ball-end screw contacts a
small groove cut into the ﬂoor of the chamber, opposite the window ﬂange above, to center the
platform and allow for ﬁne adjustment of the platform’s tilt to match the laser focal plane. Finally,
two spheres contact the back wall of the chamber’s interior, fully constraining the platform in both
rotation and translation. A sample plate (i.e., the substrate upon which L-PBF is performed) is
bolted to the build platform, and the glass slide and its holder are placed atop the platform. The
build platform, sample, and slide can thus be easily removed and replaced with high repeatability.


2.2  Inert gas ﬂow


Achieving high quality L-PBF requires a steady, uniform ﬂow of inert gas across the build area
[25, 26, 27]. Regions of low speed ﬂow below a certain threshold must be avoided, as even
momentary local stagnation can result in defects due to inadequate removal of the melt-induced
vapor plume and spatter. It has been recommended that a minimum gas velocity of 1 - 2 m/s over
the powder bed is required to obtain optimal L-PBF quality [27, 28, 29]. Although an even faster
ﬂow may be beneﬁcial [25, 30, 31, 26, 27], at a certain velocity the gas ﬂow will begin to disturb
the powder bed below, which is undesirable. To this end, Shen et al. [28], building upon earlier


                                           4work by Kalman et al. [32], modeled and validated the upper bound velocity that will not disturb
the powder bed. Therefore, a ﬁrst step in our design process was to determine a target gas velocity
for ﬂow within the HPLM chamber. Following the above guidance, this was established to be
3.1 m/s, for 15 - 45 µm stainless steel powder (SS316L).

One unique challenge arises as a result of the small size of the pressure chamber. Some amount of
local recirculation is common in L-PBF, as the gas ﬂow spreads and is not always fully captured
by the exit port. Recirculating gas in the chamber may carry with it soot and particles from the
melt pool, which may cross the path of the laser, deposit on the laser window, or alight on the
powder bed [24, 26, 33]. Most commercial L-PBF printers use build chambers with several inches
or more of vertical space between the build plate and the laser window above, and ample lateral
margin around the build area. In our much smaller chamber, any recirculation near the window is
much more likely to deposit soot onto the window surface, which may attenuate and scatter laser
energy and/or cause thermal damage to the window itself.

Toward preventing recirculation, Chen [33] and Saunders [29] both suggest a secondary ﬂow be
established with a second nozzle near the top of the chamber. This can be seen in some
commercial L-PBF machines, usually positioned near the laser optical window at the top of the
chamber. In the present study, a representation of the chamber, build platform, and a simple
nozzle were modeled using COMSOL Multiphysics software, and various strategies to prevent
recirculation were modeled, including baﬄes, guide vanes, tapering (funneling) the ﬂow path, and
enlarging the outlet port. Each of these approaches merely shifted the location at which the gas
stream splits and recirculates. However, the aforementioned secondary nozzle approach was found
to successfully prevent a low pressure region from forming and causing recirculation near the
HPLM chamber window. This solution is illustrated in parts a and b of Figure 3. The ﬁnal design
was detailed in CAD (Solidworks) and brought into COMSOL via an integration module
(Solidworks LiveLink). The critical dimensions were deﬁned as the nozzle heights and widths (W1,
H1, W2, H2), proportional entrance area at the split plane (H3/H4), and lengths (L1, L2). These
were parametrically varied in the model, and design variations were judged on the velocity
achieved above the entire print area, subject to the requirement for no recirculation near the laser
window and the desire to minimize overall gas usage (max 15 NLPM). The simulated ﬂow ﬁeld
through the ﬁnal nozzle design and chamber is shown in Figure 3c. A physical model was printed
with a Form2 3D printer (Formlabs) and attached to the gas ﬂow system as shown in Figure 3d.
Fan (GM816, Amgaze) and hot wire (405i, Testo) anemometers were used to measure gas speeds
at distances up to three inches away from both (top and bottom) nozzle outlets. It was found that
with an input ﬂow of 12 - 15 NLPM, the ﬁnal nozzle design produces gas velocities greater than
1.4 m/s above the entire print area under ambient conditions.

2.3  Gas delivery system


A ﬂow-through system was devised using a standard Ultra High Purity (UHP) argon bottle with a
regulator to supply inert gas to the chamber at pressures as high as the rated pressure of the
chamber. The system diagram is shown in Figure 4a. Needle valves upstream and downstream of
the chamber allow the user to set both the pressure and ﬂow of the argon stream within the
operating limits of the system. A large ﬁlter rated to remove 95% of 10 nm diameter particles
(United Filtration Systems, SLH818) protects equipment further downstream while adding
minimal pressure drop to the system. A ﬂowmeter calibrated for argon (Sierra Instruments,
M100H1), reads out the mass ﬂow through the system at a range of 10 - 1100 NLPM with 1%FS
accuracy, which accommodates performance at pressures up to 1200 psig. A smaller ﬂowmeter
(Sierra Instruments, M100L) can be swapped in to measure up to 50 NLPM with 1%FS accuracy
for near-atmospheric experiments. Finally, an oxygen gas sensor (Vernier) measures oxygen
content from the exhaust before it is piped to the building ventilation system.

For any desired experimental chamber pressure, a certain mass ﬂow of gas through the entire
system is required to establish the desired ﬂow velocity over the build area. The backpressure
resulting from that ﬂow in the chamber with valve 2 fully open must then be minimized to enable
the largest possible operable range of pressures and ﬂows in the system. In Figure 4b, the system’s
ﬂow resistance is measured with the built-in ﬂowmeter and pressure gauge and ﬁt to a second-order
curve. This curve is then extrapolated to show the full operating range of the system in Figure 4c.
Starting with valve 1 fully closed and the valve 2 fully open, opening valve 1 gradually moves the
system’s operating point outward along the blue curve, and closing valve 2 changes the resistance

2.4  Laser scanning system


A custom-built mirror-based 2D scanning head is used to focus and direct the output of a ﬁber

  ABSTRACT

   Powder bed additive manufacturing (AM) processes, including binder jetting (BJAM) and powder bed fusion (PBF), can manufacture com-
    plex three-dimensional components from a variety of materials. A fundamental understanding of the spreading of thin powder layers is
    essential to develop robust process parameters for powder bed AM and to assess the influence of powder feedstock characteristics on the
    subsequent process outcomes. Toward meeting these needs, this work presents the design, fabrication, and qualification of a testbed for mod-
     ular, mechanized, multi-layer powder spreading. The testbed is designed to replicate the operating conditions of commercial AM equipment,
    yet features full control over motion parameters including the translation and rotation of a roller spreading tool and precision motion of
    a feed piston and the build platform. The powder spreading mechanism is interchangeable and therefore can be customized, including the
    capability for dispensing of fine, cohesive powders using a vibrating hopper. Validation of the resolution and accuracy of the machine and its
    subsystems, as well as the spreading of exemplary layers from a range of powder sizes typical of BJAM and PBF processes, are described. The
    precision engineered testbed can therefore enable the optimization of powder spreading parameters for AM and correlation to build process
    parameters in future work, as well as exploration of spreading of specialized powders for AM and other techniques.

## pqac-00000059

From text 'skacelik2026experimentalandcomputational pages 1-4'.

Radek Skácelík, Václav Vrzal, Miroslav Španiel, and Michal Bartošák. Experimental and computational study on the influence of recoater geometry, recoating speed, and layer thickness on recoater collision. Jun 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18515-6, doi:10.1007/s00170-026-18515-6. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt attributes LPBF recoater collisions primarily to thermally induced distortion and local protrusions that raise the build surface above the available clearance. Thin-walled or low-stiffness features are especially susceptible. If vertical displacement exceeds the recoater gap, blade contact can occur; the resulting powder disturbance and blade dynamics may extend the damage laterally and compromise the layer. Recoater geometry and compliance affect the effective recoating margin: the study compares compliant rubber and rigid ceramic blades, finding that the compliant blade produced little mechanical stress on the part even when its clearance gap was fully closed. Recoating kinematics, including speed, also influence layer uniformity and the balance between cooling and thermal accumulation, although the supplied pages do not provide a specific quantitative speed trend. Likewise, the excerpt does not state a specific layer-thickness effect, but identifies clearance and layer-wise displacement as governing factors; longer cooling time reduced collision-related build failure. Spatter deposits and curled edges are not discussed explicitly in the supplied excerpt. They can therefore only be related generally to the described mechanism: as surface asperities or protrusions, they reduce clearance and can trigger blade contact, powder disturbance, and ultimately a recoater crash. The paper accounts for near-surface asperities through experimentally measured collision thresholds rather than explicitly modeling them.

## pqac-00000060

From text 'skacelik2026experimentalandcomputational pages 21-26'.

Radek Skácelík, Václav Vrzal, Miroslav Španiel, and Michal Bartošák. Experimental and computational study on the influence of recoater geometry, recoating speed, and layer thickness on recoater collision. Jun 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18515-6, doi:10.1007/s00170-026-18515-6. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt identifies recoater collision as a consequence of printed-part deformation and local overheight features exceeding the available clearance beneath the recoater. Repeated blade contact can permanently deflect thin parts, mechanically jam them, detach newly deposited layers, disturb the powder bed, and ultimately terminate the build. Thermal effects are important: insufficient cooling raises part temperature, reduces stiffness, and promotes deformation or protrusion from the powder bed. Extending the stabilization/cooling period before recoating prevented collisions in the reported experiment, whereas the original timing produced defects. Recoater geometry strongly affects mechanical loading: the rigid ceramic blade generated collision and rebound marks, while the compliant rubber blade did not impose significant mechanical stress even when the gap was fully closed. The rubber-blade test instead failed from inadequate cooling and thermal buildup. The excerpt does not provide a direct, isolated parametric comparison of recoating speed or nominal layer thickness. It reports tests at 15 and 20 µm and shows that a modified timing cycle and longer cooling interval eliminated collisions, while the original cycle caused them. In general, thicker or faster-deposited layers could increase overheight and reduce available clearance, but that specific effect is not quantified here. Spatter deposits and curled edges are not explicitly discussed in these pages; they would act as local surface asperities or upward-curled overhangs that exceed clearance and create impact initiation sites.

## pqac-00000061

From text 'astarita2026powderspreadingand pages 5-7'.

A. Astarita. Powder spreading and layer deposition in metal powder bed fusion. ArXiv, Jun 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.22989, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.22989. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt identifies recoater collisions and crashes as consequences of insufficient clearance, protruding particles, previously consolidated features, and unstable or nonuniform powder deposition. Layer thickness is central: when the recoater-to-substrate gap approaches the largest particle size, particles can become trapped beneath the recoater, causing blockage, jamming, local disturbances, reduced packing density, and poor surface coverage. Thicker layers provide more clearance and generally improve transport and spreading stability, although they require more melt energy and can reduce dimensional accuracy. Recoater velocity also affects collision risk indirectly. Low speeds allow particles to rearrange and produce more uniform deposits, whereas high speeds increase inertial transport, variability, roughness, segregation, accumulation zones, and uncovered regions; these conditions can leave obstacles or unstable powder piles in the recoater path. Geometry and material are similarly important. Rigid metallic blades can mechanically strike protruding particles or consolidated features, potentially disturbing the layer and interrupting the process. Flexible polymer blades accommodate minor irregularities and reduce collision risk, while rollers compact powder and alter rearrangement and segregation behavior. The excerpt does not specifically describe curled edges or spatter deposits as crash mechanisms, but it notes that gas flow can redistribute loose particles and create local bed morphology variations, which may contribute to obstacles encountered during recoating.

The excerpt frames recoater collision in LPBF as an interaction between the moving recoater and a part or deposited surface that enters the recoater’s travel path. The experimental fixture was deliberately designed so that accidental contact would deflect the sample away from the blade, indicating that collision risk depends on the relative trajectories, part orientation, and leading-edge geometry. Recoater geometry was varied using rubber and ceramic blades to quantify differences in recoating pressure; the excerpt does not report the comparative collision results. Layer thickness was varied from the nominal 20 µm down to 5 µm, allowing collision thresholds to be studied as the available clearance or powder-layer condition changes. Recoating speed was varied from 20 to 200 mm/s for the L-shaped specimens, with constant nominal layer thickness, to assess speed-dependent changes in frictional interaction and collision response. Sample geometries included sharp or modified edges, different contact widths, angled edges, and cylindrical surfaces; an edge parallel to the blade was considered the worst alignment. The excerpt provides partial information relevant to recoater crashes in LPBF, but it does not explicitly discuss spatter deposits or curled edges. It indicates that collision-like problems can arise when force conditions vary strongly, particularly while spreading over a prefabricated part surface; this can obstruct particle flow through the gap between the recoater and surface. Recoater geometry affects contact and jamming: straight or sharp-edge blades provide point contact, produce rougher or less dense beds, and sharp edges are associated with frequent particle jamming. Chamfered and roller recoaters provide plane contact and press particles down, although geometry and surface conditions can still influence clearance. Roller speed affects spreading behavior and roughness: a non-rotating roller gives minimum roughness, while rotation increases roughness, especially in the CW direction. Changes in rotational direction can also cause abrupt changes in powder mass, throughput, and porosity. Layer thickness is relevant because smaller thicknesses can promote particle jamming, whereas larger layer thickness reduces jamming. The excerpt notes density fluctuations near the front and rear of the layer due to silo and recycling-chamber effects, which may create local irregularities, but it does not identify spatter accumulation or curled part edges as direct crash mechanisms.

The excerpt indicates that LPBF chamber design must maintain an inert, low-humidity environment because reactive powders and alloys can oxidise or interact with moisture during processing. Oxidised powder is associated with fatigue failure and reduced toughness and tensile properties. The text describes inerting the chamber by displacing ambient gases with argon, including vacuum-swing inerting, and explains that reduced pressure can also remove humidity from the chamber, silos, and powder. Moisture can decompose under laser exposure into hydrogen and oxygen; oxygen may oxidise powder and alter build properties, while hydrogen can enter aluminium alloy lattices, cause embrittlement, and produce gas porosity in molten aluminium. However, this excerpt does not discuss the effect of chamber-wall material, does not compare stainless steel with aluminium chambers, and provides no information about galvanic corrosion between aluminium powder and a 6061 aluminium chamber. It also does not address the compatibility, swelling, degradation, or contamination risk of FKM O-rings in contact with aluminium powder. function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of LPBF subsystem failure modes reported in literature, with columns: Subsystem, Failure Mode/Problem, Reported Impact/Severity, Key References. Cover: 1) Protective window (spatter/condensate contamination, focal shift, power loss), 2) Gas flow (non-uniformity, recirculation, insufficient velocity), 3) Recoater (blade wear, collisions with spatter/curled edges, streaking), 4) Powder spreading (short feed, segregation, electrostatic charging), 5) Build piston/plate (seal friction, powder leakage), 6) Atmosphere (oxygen/moisture ingress), 7) Optics (thermal lensing, drift), 8) Z-axis (positioning accuracy). Include quantitative values where available from the evidence gathered."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Subsystem | Failure mode / problem | Reported impact / severity | Key references |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protective window | Metal condensate, soot, and spatter deposit on the process window or sacrificial slide; contamination is spatially nonuniform and can become a local absorber. | For contaminated fused silica at **400 W**, about **0.5% additional absorptivity** produced a simulated **−21.6 mm focal shift**; experiments measured approximately **−22 to −30 mm**, while beam-waist radius increased from **35 to 53 µm**. Direct transmission loss was below an estimated **1%**, but focal shift and beam degradation were more consequential. Continued heating can damage or burn the window. Gas-knife or down-draft protection, cooling, sacrificial glass, and inspection after each build are reported controls. | Bonhoff et al.; Griggs et al.; Revanur (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000054) |
| Gas flow | Insufficient local velocity, inlet-to-outlet velocity decay, stagnation, reverse flow, and recirculation; recoater position and chamber geometry alter the flow field. Small chambers have little vertical or lateral margin, making window contamination by recirculated soot more likely. | In one LPBF study, porosity stayed below **0.1% at 2.5–4.0 m/s**, whereas **≤2.0 m/s** caused sharply increased porosity, shallower and unstable melt pools, balling, necking, and swelling. Commercial measurements ranged from about **4 m/s near the inlet to 1 m/s near the outlet**. A compact testbed used a secondary upper nozzle to suppress window-side recirculation and obtained **>1.4–1.5 m/s** over the full print area at **12–15 NL/min**. Excessive velocity can entrain loose powder. | Reijonen et al.; Shen et al.; Griggs et al.; Medinilla et al. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054) |
| Recoater | Rigid-blade contact with adhered spatter, consolidated protrusions, distorted thin walls, or upward-curled edges; particle jamming where clearance approaches the largest particle diameter; damaged or nicked edges generate repeatable streaks. Literature directly quantifying HSS wear rate is sparse. | Contact can lift and excite the blade, permanently deflect thin parts, detach layers, disturb powder across the blade width, jam the mechanism, or terminate the build. Collision experiments covered **20–200 mm/s** and **5–20 µm** layers. Rigid ceramic blades produced collision and rebound marks; compliant rubber blades imposed little mechanical stress even with the gap closed. Longer cooling or stabilization prevented collisions in one experiment. | Sehhat and Mahdianikhotbesara; Whiting et al.; Oropeza et al.; Skácelík et al. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062) |
| Powder spreading and dosing | Short feed, incomplete coverage, heap segregation, agglomeration, bridging or ratholing in fine cohesive powder, and layer-density variation. Smaller particles migrate into voids and may deposit earlier, while larger particles remain near the heap front. | Higher traverse speed generally lowers packing density and coverage and increases roughness, segregation, splash, accumulation, and bare regions. Reported blade speeds extend to **150 mm/s**, while roller translation spans **5–130 mm/s**; lower speed generally improves rearrangement. Fine powders below roughly **10 µm** may be dominated by van der Waals forces. A vibrating-hopper testbed dispensed **<22 µm** steel powder, but dose depended on vibration pressure and duration and required empirical calibration. | Oropeza et al.; Sehhat and Mahdianikhotbesara; Astarita; Hou (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058) |
| Powder spreading—electrostatics | Triboelectric charging during powder–powder, powder–hopper, and powder–recoater contact; charge polarity and magnitude depend on oxide chemistry, counterface, flow rate, humidity, roughness, and particle size. Dry conditions increase persistent charge. | Electrostatic forces add to cohesion and friction; if comparable to or greater than gravity they impede flow, promote adhesion and agglomeration, and alter segregation and layer uniformity. AlSi10Mg acquired negative charge after stainless-steel contact, with reported values around **−2.80 to −5.70 nC/m²**, dependent on flow rate. Small particles can charge oppositely to large particles, enabling charge-assisted size segregation. | Alchikh-Sulaiman; Galindo et al.; Ramirez (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031) |
| Build piston and heated plate | Powder enters annular gaps and migrates past scraper or wiper seals; thermal expansion changes radial clearance and seal preload. Powder embedded at the sliding interface raises friction, stick–slip, scoring, and wear. Seal drag loads the Z drive and can produce motion hysteresis. | Peer-reviewed LPBF literature provides little quantitative service-life or leakage data for piston seals; this is mainly a machine-design and tribology risk rather than a well-quantified process result. Because commanded layers are only **30–50 µm**, micron-scale stick–slip or plate rocking is significant. Published research testbeds commonly use precision guided stages; one modular system specified **5 µm** minimum vertical increments. | Oropeza et al. (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057) |
| Atmosphere | Air leakage through doors, seals, feedthroughs, and low-pressure recirculation-loop regions; oxygen spikes during filter service; desorption of water from chamber surfaces and powder; humid powder introduces oxygen and hydrogen during melting. | Oxygen promotes oxide growth and changes fusion and mechanical properties. Moisture can yield oxygen and hydrogen; hydrogen causes gas porosity in molten aluminium and can embrittle high-strength Al alloys. One recirculating commercial system automatically repurged when oxygen exceeded **0.2%**, but that was a stainless-steel experiment and is not an aluminium best-practice target. Continuous low-range O₂ plus dew-point monitoring is required rather than relying on cylinder grade or chamber pressure alone. | Reijonen et al.; Revanur (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000065) |
| Optics | Absorption in contaminated transmissive optics and AR coatings generates refractive-index gradients and surface bulging; scan head, lens, mounting structure, and chamber-window temperature changes cause focal and geometric drift. | Thermal lensing changes focus, waist size, beam quality, and delivered irradiance even when transmitted-power loss is small. At **400 W** and **0.5% added absorption**, fused silica shifted focus by **−21.6 mm** and increased waist radius by about **30%**; N-FK51A shifted only about **−1.3 mm** under the modeled conditions. Temperature-controlled optics, purge or cooling, focus verification, witness coupons, and power measurement after all windows are needed. | Bonhoff et al.; Revanur (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| Z axis and layer thickness | Backlash, compliance, seal drag, stick–slip, thermal expansion, platform rocking, magnetic-coupling slip, datum disturbance after recoater contact, and insufficient settling. Open-loop focus or Z control can add dynamic error. | Z error directly changes effective layer thickness and recoater clearance; accumulated bias changes part height and energy per unit powder volume. Recoater collision can alter the datum and produce inconsistent subsequent layers. Research platforms report **5 µm** minimum stage increments, but increment size is not equivalent to absolute accuracy or repeatability. Qualification should measure bidirectional positioning, loaded repeatability, lost motion, tilt, and settling at operating temperature. | Oropeza et al.; Revanur (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057) |

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of the user's design choices that go against published best practice, with columns: Design Choice, Issue / Conflict with Best Practice, Published Recommendation (with numbers), Priority. Include:
1. Fused silica window/cover slide: worst thermal lensing material per Bonhoff; use N-FK51A or sapphire
2. 2 m/s cross-flow may be marginal: literature shows 2.0 m/s is the critical lower threshold; recommend ≥2.5 m/s
3. Small chamber (6.4L) with no secondary nozzle: prone to recirculation near window per Griggs testbed; dual-nozzle recommended
4. HSS rigid blade: higher collision risk than compliant polymer blade per Skacelik; consider rubber/silicone  
5. 200°C max preheat: inadequate for crack-susceptible 2xxx/7xxx alloys; 500°C needed for 6xxx per Riener
6. 8mm hopper outlet slot: narrow slot + fine cohesive Al powder = bridging risk; widen or add vibration
7. Bare 6061-T6 Al chamber: potential powder-chamber cross-contamination when screening different alloys; stainless recommended
8. Vacuum purging to 1 mbar then backfill: may leave residual moisture on chamber walls; consider heated purge or multiple vacuum-backfill cycles"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Design Choice | Issue / Conflict with Best Practice | Published Recommendation (with numbers) | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fused-silica chamber window plus 3 mm fused-silica sacrificial slide | Contamination makes fused silica strongly thermo-optically sensitive. At 400 W and 0.5% added absorption, modeling gave a −21.6 mm focus shift; contaminated-window experiments measured approximately −22 to −30 mm and beam-waist growth from 35 to 53 µm. | Use a replaceable, AR-coated sacrificial shield and gas knife, monitor transmitted power/focus, and clean or replace between builds. N-FK51A produced only about −1.3 mm modeled shift under comparable conditions. Sapphire is defensible for the structural pressure window because of toughness and NIR transmission, but the cited literature does **not** establish it as thermally superior to N-FK51A. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000054) | **Critical** |
| Nominal cross-flow of about 2 m/s | About 2.0 m/s is a reported lower critical threshold, not a comfortable design point; local speed will be lower where inlet profiles decay or recirculation occurs. At 2.5–4.0 m/s, reported porosity remained below 0.1%; at ≤2.0 m/s, porosity, unstable melt pools, balling, necking, and swelling increased. | Design for a **measured local velocity of at least 2.5 m/s everywhere over the usable plate**, preferably with adjustment through roughly 2.5–4.0 m/s, while verifying that the upper setting does not pick up Al powder. Qualify using a 2-D velocity map rather than slot-area flow calculations. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | **Critical** |
| Compact 6.4 L chamber with only the plate-level cross-flow/gas knife | Compact chambers have little vertical and lateral margin; recirculated soot can cross the beam, redeposit on the bed, or foul the window. Baffles, guide vanes, tapering, and a larger outlet merely shifted recirculation in one small-chamber study. | Add an independently adjustable **secondary upper nozzle/window sweep** and a generously captured outlet. Griggs et al. suppressed window-side recirculation with dual nozzles and achieved >1.4–1.5 m/s over a 10 × 60 mm area using 12–15 NL/min; the present LPBF process should instead meet the ≥2.5 m/s local target established above. Validate with CFD followed by smoke/PIV/hot-wire mapping. (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054) | **Critical** |
| Rigid high-speed-steel recoater blade | A rigid blade transmits collision loads from adhered spatter, overheight tracks, and curled parts; a nick creates a repeatable longitudinal streak. Rigid ceramic blades produced collision/rebound marks, whereas compliant rubber imposed little stress even when clearance closed. | Provide interchangeable rigid and compliant cartridges. Use a compliant silicone/rubber or other proven polymer blade for early development and collision-prone alloys, with a rigid blade retained for controlled comparison. Operate initially near **50–100 mm/s**, below the proposed 150 mm/s maximum, and add blade-height adjustment, force/accelerometer monitoring, and automatic abort. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060) | **High** |
| Build-plate heating limited to 200 °C | This range is useful for AlSi10Mg stress management but should not be presented as sufficient for crack-prone wrought alloys. For 7075, 100–200 °C did not significantly reduce cracking; 400 °C caused columnar crack networks and lower hardness. For Zr-modified 6182, fully equiaxed, crack-free material with >99.0% density was demonstrated at 500 °C. | Either restrict the first machine’s claims to AlSi10Mg/Al-Mg-Sc-Zr and grain-refined alloys proven at ≤200 °C, or redesign the hot module for alloy-dependent operation up to about **500 °C**. Do not extrapolate the 6182 result to every 2xxx/6xxx/7xxx alloy; high-temperature preheating alone did not solve 7075 cracking. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042) | **High** |
| Gravity-fed wedge hopper with an 8 mm outlet and fluted metering roller | Fine Al powder is cohesive; van der Waals, capillary, and electrostatic forces promote arching, ratholing, wall adhesion, and intermittent short feed. An 8 mm slot may work, but the literature does not supply a transferable repeatability value proving it will work for 15–45 µm Al. | Make outlet width adjustable and use steep, smooth mass-flow walls, active agitation or a controllable vibrator, load-cell dose verification, and a low-level/short-feed interlock. Calibrate delivered mass versus actuation for every alloy and fill level. The published vibrating-hopper testbed used pressure/time calibration over **20–60 psi** and **0.5–20 s**, with three repeats per condition; its dose calculation was explicitly only first-order. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058) | **Critical** |
| Bare 6061-T6 aluminium chamber used while screening multiple aluminium alloys | The retrieved LPBF literature does not establish bare 6061 as prohibited, but soft, uncoated aluminium walls are harder to clean without scratching and can retain powder/condensate, increasing cross-alloy carry-over. A blanket claim that stainless steel is mandatory would exceed the cited evidence. | Prefer removable electropolished **316L liners**, trays, ducts, and powder-contact modules—or construct the powder-contact interior from stainless steel—while retaining aluminium externally if weight and machining favor it. Establish swab-based cleanliness acceptance and dedicated removable parts for chemically sensitive Sc/Zr, Cu-, Zn-, or Mg-bearing campaigns. | **High; engineering control with evidence gap** |
| Single evacuation to about 1 mbar followed by argon backfill | Pressure alone does not verify dryness: water desorbs from powder, porous insulation, seals, and chamber surfaces after backfill and heating. Moisture can supply oxygen and hydrogen; hydrogen promotes porosity in molten Al and can embrittle high-strength Al alloys. | Use multiple evacuation/backfill cycles, dry-argon flow-through during warm-up, and—where materials permit—mild chamber bakeout. Measure rather than infer atmosphere quality: install low-range O₂ and dew-point sensors near the return and interlock laser operation to validated limits. Keep slight positive pressure during processing, but pressure must not substitute for O₂/H₂O measurement. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000065) | **Critical** |

info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)

- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)

quotes, additional tags, etc.).

so that the artifact is properly contextualized.

Use the tools to answer the question: We are designing a small research laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, grain-refined 2xxx/6xxx/7xxx) from 50-300 g powder lots. The current design: a 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser (1070 nm); a 2-axis galvanometer scanner with an f = 160 mm f-theta lens (about 75 um spot) above a 50.8 x 8 mm fused-silica window in the lid, with a removable 3 mm fused-silica cover slide swept by a gas knife; a bare 6061-T6 aluminium chamber of 280 x 190 x 120 mm (about 6.4 L) sealed with FKM 75A O-ring face seals, vacuum-purged with a dry scroll pump to about 1 mbar, back-filled with argon 5.0 and run at +5 to +20 mbar with a recirculating sealed blower, cyclone and HEPA filter, giving about 2 m/s cross-flow through 120 x 8 mm slots across the plate; interchangeable heated build modules (25, 50 or 75 mm diameter plates, 40 mm stroke) with 24 V cartridge heaters to 200 C in a 6061 heater block, a Macor standoff thermal break, an aramid-felt plus carbon-filled-PTFE scraper seal on a cooler piston head, a carbon-filled-PTFE rim wiper on the plate, the plate held on a bayonet (a pull-stud drawbar is planned), and a magnetic Z coupling; a dose-from-above fluted-roller metering base fed by swappable 38-233 cm3 stainless wedge hoppers with 8 mm outlet slots; a high-speed-steel blade on a ball-screw recoater at about 50-150 mm/s with 30-50 um layers; a drop-down chamber door for robot access.

Please review the peer-reviewed literature (and machine-builder documentation where it is the only source), with citations and quantitative values:
1. For each subsystem above, which failure modes and operating problems are reported for research, open-architecture and desktop LPBF machines: powder leaking past build pistons and into the gaps around heated plates; piston seal friction, stick-slip and wear; recoater blade wear, nicks and streaking; short feed; recoater collisions with spatter or curled edges; vibration-induced powder bed defects; spatter and condensate on the window and cover slide and the resulting focal shift or power loss; cross-flow non-uniformity and recirculation in small chambers; oxygen and moisture ingress; heater and thermocouple failures; thermal drift of the optics; Z-axis positioning accuracy and layer-thickness error; electrostatic charging of powder.

3. LPBF machines that dose powder from above (hopper and roller or slot) instead of a supply piston: reported dose repeatability, segregation, bridging or ratholing of fine Al powder, and flow through narrow slots.
4. Very small build plates (25-75 mm): reported edge effects in packing density near the cylinder wall, heat accumulation, gas-flow effects, and how much of the plate is usable for test specimens.
5. The highest-priority changes you would recommend before this design is built.

Abstract:

 Additive manufacturing (AM) enables new possibilities for the design and manufacturing of complex metal architectures. Incorporating lattice structures into complex part geometries can enhance strength-to-weight and surface area-to-volume ratios for valuable components, particularly in industries such as medical devices and aerospace. However, lattice structures and their interconnections may result in unsupported down-skin surfaces, potentially limiting their manufacturability by metal AM technologies, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). This study aimed at examining the correlation between down-skin surface area and the manufacturability of lattice structures fabricated using LPBF. Image processing algorithms were used to analyze down-skin surface areas of seven unique lattice designs and to devise quantitative metrics (such as down-skin surface area, discrete surface count, surface inter-connectivity, down-skin ratio, over-print/under-print volumes, etc.) to evaluate LPBF manufacturability. The seven lattice designs were subsequently manufactured using maraging steel via LPBF, and then examined using imaging using X-ray micro-computed tomography (XCT). The geometric accuracy of the lattice designs was compared with XCT scans of the manufactured lattices by employing a voxel-based image comparison technique. The results indicated a strong relationship between down-skin surface area, surface interconnectivity, and the manufacturability of a given lattice design. The digital manufacturability evaluation workflow was also applied to a medical device design, further affirming its potential industrial utility for complex geometries.

Abstract:
Real-time process monitoring is essential for achieving consistent part quality in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF), yet robust and practical defect prediction frameworks remain underdeveloped. This study presents a machine learning-based approach for predicting unstable melt pool conditions, leveraging an open dataset of melt pool variability measurements from Ti-6Al-4V builds on an EOS M290 system. The framework utilizes fundamental process parameters—laser velocity, power, scan orientation, and track location—combined with statistical melt pool geometry features to train a Random Forest classifier. The model achieved an accuracy of 99.79% in distinguishing between stable and unstable melt pool states, with balanced sensitivity and specificity. Analysis of defect trends across the process parameter space revealed that higher scan velocities and certain orientations significantly increase defect likelihood. The results confirm that interpretable, computationally efficient machine learning models can provide robust real-time defect prediction using features already accessible on commercial LPBF platforms. The framework offers a scalable and industry-relevant pathway toward enhanced quality assurance in metal additive manufacturing, supporting the advancement of intelligent, closed-loop LPBF process control.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The use of components fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) requires the development of processing parameters that can produce high-quality material. Manipulating the most commonly identified critical build parameters (e.g., laser power, laser scan speed, and layer thickness) on LPBF equipment can generate acceptable parts for established materials and moderately intricate part geometries. The need to fabricate increasingly complex parts from unique materials drives the limited research into LPBF process control using underutilized parameters, such as atmosphere composition and pressure. As presented in this review, manipulating atmosphere composition and pressure in laser beam welding has been shown to expand processing windows and produce higher-quality welds. The similarities between laser beam welding and laser-based AM processes suggest that this atmosphere control research could be effectively adapted for LPBF, an area that has not been widely explored. Tailoring this research for LPBF has significant potential to reveal novel processing regimes. This review presents the current state of the art in atmosphere research for laser beam welding and LPBF, with a focus on studies exploring cover gas composition and pressure, and concludes with an outlook on future LPBF atmosphere control systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is rapidly developing as a principal method for the manufacture of metal parts. However, widespread adoption of the technology, especially for safety-critical applications, is impeded by complications to achieving the desired component quality and reliability. Spatter occurs due to interactions between the laser and the melt pool and involves the ejection of material from within or about its vicinity. Recognized as a process signature in L-PBF, spatter is considered detrimental to build quality. However, relationships between spatter kinetics and part defects have remained largely underexplored. In this investigation, spatter is evaluated via in situ optical tomography (OT) imaging acquired during builds performed with Ti6Al4V powder. Results showed that the volume of spatter content is greater at particular scan angles as well as specific locations in the build chamber. Furthermore, the spatter dynamics behave differently upwind and downwind of printed regions and indicate that local variations in gas flow can be inferred from spatter signatures. As spatter is known to directly cause defects in parts produced by L-PBF, regions with increased spatter potentially signal reduced metal quality. Variations in the spatter content are identified and regions of the build at greater risk for defects are highlighted.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Shielding gas flow in metal Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) removes ejecta and byproducts from the build plate and the optical path, preventing laser interference and loss of part quality. Previous research conducted on an EOS M290 used Magnetic Resonance Velocimetry (MRV) to resolve the three-component, three-dimensional flow field and identified a region of recirculation below the lower vent. The present work demonstrates the correction of this recirculation through practical chamber modifications: raising the build platform and optical assembly, and redesigning the recoater and the lower inlet to reflect the new build plate position. MRV was leveraged to generate flow distribution maps and velocity profiles of the modified configuration, showing a marked change in the overall flow field. Plate scans across the build area characterized the impact of gas flow improvements on process response. Specimens from the original configuration showed progressively shallower melt pools toward the vent, whereas those from the modified configuration exhibited a ~10% higher average melt pool depth in the region most affected by prior recirculation. Qualification artifacts built under both conditions provided preliminary evidence of improved part performance via enhanced gas flow distribution. These results highlight potential benefits of uniform gas flow distribution across the build plate through simple EOS M290 chamber modifications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is of great importance for the visual measurement and analysis of the metallization process, which is the process of solid, liquid, and gas phase transformations of metal powders under high-energy laser irradiation due to the low boiling point/high saturated vapor pressure. Since the evaporation of metals involves the interaction of driving forces such as vapor back pressure, surface tension, and gravity, the movement of the melt pool is not stable. At the same time, it also produces vaporization products such as vapor plumes and sprays, which cause defects such as bubbles, porosity, lack of fusion, inclusions, etc., during the manufacturing process of the parts, affecting the performance and manufacturing quality of the parts. More and more researchers are using imaging technologies, such as high-speed X-ray, high-speed visible light cameras, and high-speed schlieren imaging, to perform noncontact visual measurements and analyses of the melt pool, vapor plume, and spatter during the metal evaporation process, and the results show that the metal evaporation process can be suppressed by optimizing the process parameters and changing the processing atmosphere, thereby reducing part defects and improving part performance and built part quality. This paper reviews the research on metal evaporation mechanisms and visual measurement methods of metal evaporation, then discusses the measures of metal evaporation, and finally summarizes and prospects the future research hotspots of LPBF technology, according to the existing scholars’ research on numerical simulation analysis and visual measurement methods of the metal evaporation process.

Abstract:
Powder spattering and splashing in the melt pool are common phenomena during Laser-based Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) of metallic materials having high fluidity. For this purpose, analytical and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models have been deduced for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The single printed layer’s dimensions were estimated using primary operating conditions for the analytical model. In CFD modelling, the volume of fluid and discrete element modelling techniques were applied to illustrate the splashing and spatter phenomena, providing a novel hydrodynamics CFD model for LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The computational results were compared with the experimental analyses. A trial-and-error method was used to propose an optimized set of parameters for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. Laser scanning speed, laser spot diameter and laser power were changed. On the other hand, the powder layer thickness and hatch distance were kept constant. Following on, 20 samples were fabricated using the LPBF process. The printed samples’ microstructures were used to select optimized parameters for achieving defect-free parts. It was found that the recoil pressure, vaporization, high-speed vapor cloud, Marangoni flow, hydraulic pressure and buoyancy are all controlled by the laser-material interaction time. As the laser-AlSi10Mg material interaction period progresses, the forces presented above become dominant. Splashing occurs due to a combination of increased recoil pressure, laser-material interaction time, higher material’s fluidity, vaporization, dominancy of Marangoni flow, high-speed vapor cloud, hydraulic pressure, buoyancy, and transformation of keyhole from J-shape to reverse triangle-shape that is a tongue-like protrusion in the keyhole. In the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy, only the conduction mode melt flow has been determined. For multi-layers printing of AlSi10Mg alloy, the optimum operating conditions are laser power = 140 W, laser spot diameter = 180 µm, laser scanning speed = 0.6 m/s, powder layer thickness = 50 µm and hatch distance = 112 µm. These conditions have been identified using sample microstructures.

However, industrial adoption remains limited due to insufficient understanding of the complex interplay among materials, processes, designs, and performance. Existing reviews lack an integrated analytical framework; thus, this study pioneers a closed-loop “Material-Process-Design-Performance (MPDP)” framework for critical analysis. We systematically categorize aerospace-relevant composite systems and core AM technologies, emphasizing their interactions and constraints. Finally, we propose a strategic development pathway to guide future research and industrial translation, particularly for next-generation aircraft and spacecraft systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
With concerns about climate change, nature-based solutions for flood risk management have been increasing in popularity across Europe, and targeting headwater streams can be an effective approach by increasing forest floodplains through inundation of surrounding areas. However, accurately measuring stream discharge remains a challenge. One promising method is to measure the surface velocity and apply a surface velocity coefficient. This study investigates the determination of surface velocity coefficient in headwater streams using the float and current meter methods. The relationship between surface velocity coefficient and relative submergence (ratio of water depth to roughness height) is analysed. The results support prior modelling results that the surface velocity coefficient decreases with relative submergence and extend the range of prior work for very small relative submergence, using experimental and field observations. The surface velocity coefficient was observed to decrease from 0.85 to 0.53 as relative submergence decreased from 270000 in a smooth glass laboratory channel to 0.093 in a field setting. Field discharge measurements upstream of a channel-spanning engineered logjam were used to show used to predict local inundation and the uncertainty is reported.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is an additive manufacturing technology that is gaining increasing interest in aerospace, automotive and biomedical applications due to the possibility of processing lightweight alloys such as AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V. Both these alloys have microstructures and mechanical properties that are strictly related to the type of heat treatment applied after the L-PBF process. The present review aimed to summarize the state of the art in terms of the microstructural morphology and consequent mechanical performance of these materials after different heat treatments. While optimization of the post-process heat treatment is key to obtaining excellent mechanical properties, the first requirement is to manufacture high quality and fully dense samples. Therefore, effects induced by the L-PBF process parameters and build platform temperatures were also summarized. In addition, effects induced by stress relief, annealing, solution, artificial and direct aging, hot isostatic pressing, and mixed heat treatments were reviewed for AlSi10Mg and Ti6AlV samples, highlighting variations in microstructure and corrosion resistance and consequent fracture mechanisms.
